title: Open letter: a library's centenary
stem:
An open letter published in a regional newspaper on the hundredth anniversary of a public library, written by its current head librarian.

To the people who built this library, a hundred years ago today,

You will not know me. When you laid the foundation stone in 1926, you could not have imagined a woman holding my job, or a building where children borrow laptops alongside picture books, or a queue on winter mornings of people who come simply because it is warm.

You carved four words above the door: KNOWLEDGE FREELY GIVEN HERE. Some of my colleagues call that old-fashioned. I disagree. In an age when answers are sold by the click and attention by the second, those four words read less like a motto and more like a dare.

Our budget is a third of what it was fifteen years ago. Our opening hours have shrunk. And still, last year, 212,000 people walked through your door.

So I am writing to you, who cannot answer, because the people who can answer need to hear it: the promise you carved is still being kept. For now.

With respect and gratitude,
The Head Librarian

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Analyse how the writer uses the letter form and its unusual addressee to achieve her purpose.
markscheme: addressing the long-dead founders is an apostrophe that creates dignity and a sense of history
dual audience: ostensibly the founders, actually readers and decision-makers ('the people who can answer')
respectful formal register and sign-off build ethos
reveals purpose indirectly: a plea against funding cuts framed as gratitude
final minor sentence 'For now.' creates an ominous twist and urgency
open-letter publication turns private address into public argument

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Examine how the letter uses the contrast between past and present contexts.
markscheme: contrast of 1926 expectations with present (woman librarian, laptops) shows social change and progress
the carved motto reread in a new context of reception: from 'old-fashioned' to 'a dare'
critique of the digital attention economy ('sold by the click') contrasts with the free civic ideal
statistics (a third of the budget, 212,000 visitors) set decline in funding against continued need – logos
people coming 'because it is warm' hints at contemporary poverty, widening the library's social role
the past is used as moral authority to judge present decisions
